title: Trump Orders Navy to Rip Out Electromagnetic Catapults, Return to Steam on Aircraft Carriers
excerpt: A national security memorandum directs the Navy to abandon the Ford-class electromagnetic launch system and revert to steam catapults, a move that could cost billions and reverse years of development.
body:
• Trump signed a national security memorandum directing the Navy to remove electromagnetic catapults from future Ford-class aircraft carriers and revert to steam-powered systems.
  • The order applies to the fourth Ford-class carrier, USS Doris Miller (CVN-81), and all subsequent ships. The first three ships — Ford, Kennedy, and Enterprise — will retain the electromagnetic system.
  • General Atomics, the EMALS manufacturer, said its work on the Doris Miller is nearly 50% complete and warned the reversal would introduce "significant cost, schedule, and integration risks."
  • China and France are both adopting electromagnetic catapults for their newest carriers, raising questions about whether the US is ceding a technological edge.

A Decade-Long Grudge Becomes Policy

President Trump signed a national security memorandum on Thursday ordering the Navy to tear out the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) from future aircraft carriers and replace it with steam catapults — a technology the Navy phased out more than 15 years ago.

The directive makes good on a promise Trump first made in 2017, when he told Time magazine that he had instructed the Navy to go back to "goddamn steam" after hearing a sailor praise the old system during a ship visit. Navy leaders and defense contractors have resisted the idea ever since, citing the enormous cost and engineering challenges of reversing a system that was designed into the Ford class from the ground up.

"Billions of dollars more they spent on electric catapults and they're not good. They're not nearly as good, too complex."

— President Donald Trump, defense summit in Pennsylvania

What Changes — and What Doesn't

The memorandum directs the Navy to redesign the fourth ship in the Ford class, the USS Doris Miller (CVN-81), and all subsequent carriers. The first three ships — the USS Gerald R. Ford, John F. Kennedy, and Enterprise — will keep their electromagnetic systems.

The Doris Miller is not expected to enter the fleet until 2034, but the Navy plans to lay its keel this year. General Atomics, the company that builds EMALS and the Advanced Arresting Gear, said its work on the Doris Miller is nearly 50% complete and warned that changing course now would create "significant cost, schedule, and integration risks."

The Cost and Engineering Challenge

Replacing electromagnetic catapults with steam on a carrier designed for electricity is not a simple swap. The Ford class was built from scratch around the EMALS architecture. Sections that housed steam infrastructure on older Nimitz-class carriers have been reworked or eliminated entirely.

Bryan Clark, a naval expert at the Hudson Institute, said the transition would likely cost billions of dollars. He noted that the Ford's electrical system is actually cheaper to operate — about $100 million less per year than a Nimitz-class ship — and requires 500 fewer sailors in part because fewer technicians are needed for steam-related maintenance.

"Electric is more reliable," Clark said. "If I can turn these components to be electric instead of steam, it eliminates all the steam-related mechanical parts."

Geopolitical Implications

The move comes as both China and France are investing in electromagnetic catapult technology for their newest carriers. China's Type 003 Fujian carrier uses an electromagnetic system, and France plans to install EMALS on its next-generation carrier.

General Atomics warned that the decision could "create opportunities for adversaries to close the capability gap" and undermine US technological superiority at a time when strengthening the defense industrial base is a national priority.

Broader Naval Overhaul

The memorandum also includes directives beyond catapults. It calls for a new public shipyard — the first new Navy shipyard in 83 years — to accelerate submarine repair. It directs the Pentagon to pursue more foreign investment in US shipbuilding, allowing foreign shipbuilders to construct up to two ships overseas while training American workers and investing in domestic yards.

The Navy has been trying to boost submarine production for years, recently awarding General Dynamics and HII a $76.6 billion contract for nine Virginia-class and five Columbia-class submarines to be delivered by 2038.
